title: GS Holdings stock fell as Q2 revenue grew 24.8 percent - AD HOC NEWS
content: GS Holdings stock posted Q2 2026 operating profit of KRW 1.72 trillion and a 23.2 percent margin. The October 6 price was KRW 105,800 after a 0.56 percent decline. GS Holdings stock was last at KRW 105,800 on the Korea Exchange on October 6, 2026, down 0.56 percent from the prior close. The latest reported quarter showed revenue growth of 24.8 percent, giving the diversified group a stronger earnings base as it expands into AI data center infrastructure. According to ATS View, GS Holdings reported Q2 2026 revenue of KRW 7.41 trillion, up 24.8 percent from Q2 2025. Operating profit was KRW 1.72 trillion, while net income reached KRW 1.13 trillion. The operating margin was 23.2 percent in Q2 2026, compared with 18.4 percent in Q1 2026 and 8.2 percent in Q2 2025. That progression makes profitability the key link between GS Holdings' energy exposure and its retail, construction, infrastructure and services businesses. ATS View listed September 14 reports that GS Holdings planned a KRW 200 billion investment in affiliate GS AI Infra and was preparing a KRW 15 trillion AI data center project. The figures point to a capital-intensive growth path beyond the group's traditional refining and retail activities. The investment story also raises a financial question: strong quarterly cash generation must support the new infrastructure program without weakening the balance sheet. GS Holdings generated KRW 800.8 billion in operating cash flow in Q2 2026, according to the structured quarterly figures, while the company homepage describes operations spanning 30 countries and 104 subsidiaries. StockHub lists seven GS Holdings target prices, with a median of KRW 138,000 and a latest September 1 report from Heungkuk Securities carrying a Buy view and a KRW 170,000 target. The range runs from KRW 100,000 to KRW 170,000, making target dispersion a material counter-factor to the upbeat earnings trend. GS Holdings was last at KRW 105,800 on October 6, 2026, with a 52-week range of KRW 44,000 to KRW 133,200. Trading volume was 372,545 shares and market capitalization was KRW 9.8 trillion, so the stock stood below its yearly high while quarterly operating profit was materially higher than a year earlier. Georgia Southern University received approval from the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia Tuesday to establish a Doctor of Optometry (O.D.) degree program. According to a release from the university, the decision authorizes the creation of Georgia’s first college of optometry at Georgia Southern and allows the institution to offer the new degree, filling a long-standing educational and health care gap in the state. The university anticipates enrolling an inaugural class in the O.D. program in Fall 2029. “This Doctor of Optometry program, the state’s first program of its kind, represents an important investment in health care education in Georgia by expanding regional health care access and removing geographic barriers for residents seeking optometric education and care,” said Avinandan Mukherjee, Ph.D., provost and executive vice president for academic affairs at Georgia Southern. “Building on a comprehensive health care education portfolio and interprofessional experiential pedagogies at Georgia Southern, this program will serve to expand access to ocular medicine while educating future Georgia optometrists.” The new college addresses a critical need for expanded access to eye care across the state, particularly in rural and underserved communities, and as an increased demand for modern, cost-effective eye care places new pressures on the health care system. By training future optometrists in Georgia, Georgia Southern will continue to help strengthen the health care workforce pipeline and improve health outcomes for generations to come, the release stated. The Regents approval also allows Georgia Southern to recruit an inaugural dean, followed by an associate dean, assistant dean and eventually several clinical and research directors, 25 specialized faculty members and 12 support staff. The degree approval follows the allocation of $29.8 million in direct state funding through the state’s Amended Fiscal Year 2026 Budget to launch the new college at Georgia Southern. The state investment supports the comprehensive renovation of the Highway 301 facility in Statesboro, converting it into a modern academic and clinical training center specifically tailored for optometric education. This resource also expands opportunities for students to pursue careers in vision care by exposing them to a new level and quality of academic preparation and clinical rotations that have not been available to them in the state of Georgia. The program is pending final approval by the Commission on Colleges and Universities and is in stage one of accreditation with the Accreditation Council on Optometric Education. In August, Georgia Southern announced that a Optometric Education Task Force, led by Horace Deal, O.D., was established to advise on the development of the University’s College of Optometry. Together, the task force will provide strategic guidance as Georgia Southern advances planning for the college of optometry, including program proposal, curriculum development, accreditation planning, partnerships, clinical education opportunities and workforce alignment.

title: “I got no clue what happened”: LUCKI reveals stitches following ComplexCon altercation, says LAPD still has his car and $100,000 inside - Revolt TV
content: LUCKI is speaking out following the incident in which he was injured outside of ComplexCon over the weekend. On Monday (Oct. 5), the Dr*gs R Bad rapper revealed the stitches he received after Saturday’s (Oct. 3) altercation involving what appeared to be members of Playboi Carti’s entourage. LUCKI also called out the Los Angeles Police Department, which, according to him, is still in possession of several of his belongings. “Look at your baby. Aye, though, LAPD, can I please get my car back? I don’t know what happened,” he said in an Instagram Story. “I got no clue what happened. I don’t know. It’s a lot going on, but I got $100,000 in the car, my debit card.” “I don’t know if you guys [are] trying to have a little fun, but can I please get my car back?” he continued. For better or worse, LUCKI stopped short of explaining what happened during the altercation, let alone what led up to it. In case you missed it, footage from Saturday showed LUCKI and several others getting into a brawl outside of the Los Angeles Convention Center. Security could be seen trying to break up the altercation, with one witness saying, “Somebody just got stabbed. I think somebody got stabbed in the hand.” Roughly 30 seconds into the video, what appeared to be Carti opened the door of a nearby car to get a look at the fight. Shortly after, on-site personnel were heard calling for a paramedic as another person urged them to get LUCKI “to a hospital.” According to the LAPD, the fight happened at around 4:45 p.m. PT, and when officers arrived, the group “quickly dispersed.” Authorities found four people with injuries “consistent with stab wounds or lacerations,” two of whom were taken to a local hospital. “Both sustained injuries that appeared to be the result of a knife attack,” police said in a statement. A third victim made their own way to a local hospital, where they were treated for a “severe laceration believed to have been sustained during the altercation.” The fourth person suffered a laceration to his elbow but declined treatment at the scene, though it’s “unknown whether he later sought medical treatment or was transported to a hospital.” At the time of reporting, no suspects have been identified. That being said, ComplexCon addressed the incident in a statement of its own, emphasizing that it took place “on the public street outside the event.” Organizers said, “The safety and security of our guests, talent, partners, and staff is our highest priority. We are aware of an incident that occurred outside the ComplexCon event yesterday, and our security team and the LAPD responded immediately." They continued, "We take incidents of this nature extremely seriously and remain focused on maintaining a safe and secure environment for everyone attending ComplexCon.”

title: US Market Pulse October 2026 - Goldman Sachs Asset Management
content: The cyclical impulse from a trillion dollars in cumulative AI capex and trillions more in government spending has been evident in the global activity pickup. Led by strong industrial and manufacturing activity, Q3 GDP growth is tracking 3.4% in the US, 0.8% in the Euro area, and 4% in China. We expect modest acceleration in 2027 as energy headwinds fade and consumer spending adds to robust corporate investment. Core is close to target in most countries but still notably higher in the US, where goods inflation remains elevated due to boosts from tariffs and tech-flation while services have largely normalized. Goods inflation elsewhere has returned to long-run trends due to increased Chinese goods supply, while service, shelter, and labor prices pressure more in non-US DMs. Our forecasts are on the dovish side of market pricing as we expect inflation normalization to continue. We anticipate one more hike this year from the FOMC, ECB, and BoE, and then a pause to watch the data. Further hikes in 2027 would likely require a material acceleration in prices, jobs, and/or growth. Source: Bloomberg and Goldman Sachs Asset Management. As of September 30, 2026. We think the income environment remains attractive but are mindful of spread risk in credit markets, maintaining an up-in-quality bias and being selective within AI. title: Inside the Revival of Venture Capital Liquidity with an Industry Pioneer - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. As liquidity in venture capital declines, the secondary market is increasingly important for investors and companies, says Hans Swildens, partner in Goldman Sachs Asset & Wealth Management, on Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors. Swildens explains why companies are staying private longer and how artificial intelligence is creating opportunities as well as headwinds for portfolios. In this conversation with Michael Brandmeyer, global head and chief investment officer of the External Investing Group within Goldman Sachs Asset Management, Swildens also discusses the strategic rationale behind agreeing to sell his firm, Industry Ventures, to Goldman Sachs in January 2026. Hans Swildens: One thing that's interesting in our market that's starting to happen is that even participants in the secondary market are starting to get liquidity through secondaries, which historically had never happened. There's so much capital sitting in the system that it's not enough liquidity to give back all the capital into the market. And so, we think that the venture growth market, on the secondary side of the market can be larger than the primary. I think this is one of the most exciting times I've ever seen for investing. And I think we're just beginning in it. Michael Brandmeyer: Welcome to Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors. I'm Michael Brandmeyer. Venture capital has a liquidity problem. Companies are staying private longer, exits have slowed, and limited partners are asking a simple question: When do I actually get paid? My guest, Hans Swildens, built Industry Ventures around that question, growing it into a leading venture secondary specialist with roughly $7 billion in assets under supervision before agreeing to combine with Goldman Sachs Asset Management in January of 2026. Today, how severe is the venture liquidity crunch? What's real in AI? And why he finally said yes to being acquired. Michael Brandmeyer: For our listeners that may not be focused on secondaries all the time, if I'm an early entrepreneur, if I'm an early VC investor or even a later stage investor, what are the reasons that people are selling to secondary players like you? Hans Swildens: Well, the reasons have been changing over time. So, when we first started you know, 26 years ago most of it was distressed sellers, sellers that no longer wanted the investments anymore like a corporate venture capital fund decided to terminate their investments and then sell the portfolio, or a hedge fund decided to stop making private investments and just concentrate on the liquid securities and sell their private portfolio. A lot of it was distressed sellers just exiting things they didn't need or want anymore. And then that evolved over time to include sellers that had made a big gain. And I would say a vast majority of what we've been purchasing over the last 10 years has been giving gains to investors. We also have been buying portfolios at losses to the original cost as well, but I would say that that's tilted over the last 10 years so that you see sellers using the market for portfolio rebalancing or profit-taking or risk management. If a single position in their portfolio outweighs everything else, that they can trim it. More traditional portfolio management reasons to sell securities. Michael Brandmeyer: Let's go down one level to what's actually happening in existing venture capital portfolios, because if you talk to investors, be the entrepreneurs or limited partners or venture capitalists, there's just a huge illiquidity problem out there. So what's going on? Is it a problem of marks? Is it a plumbing? What are the big issues that you're seeing that are holding us back from a liquidity standpoint? Hans Swildens: I think it's everything. There's a cross current of AI growth and non-growth due to AI in the private market. So that's one issue I think. The NAV marks, some of them are undervalued, some of them are overvalued, and that's becoming more extreme of whether or not something's very overvalued or very undervalued because of the way NAV is held in the funds. I think there's also kind of concentration in the market now around certain names, and so you're seeing a lot of crowding in like the top 25 private names in the market. When you go beyond the top 25 private names and there's 30,000 private companies, the market gets pretty illiquid. And then in terms of M&A and IPO activity which has been challenged over the last five years, we're starting to see that accelerate. But there's so many illiquid companies and so much NAV is illiquid. I think McKinsey came out and said they thought it was over $1 trillion in prior funds, and then other people came out and said it's over $3 trillion in prior funds. So there's so much capital sitting in the system that even a few IPOs or let's say it normalizes to 50 or so IPOs per year that's not enough liquidity to give back all the capital into the market. So you're seeing a lot of structuring around secondaries in the primary financing events with tenders in the companies. Seeing a lot of restructuring of funds with CVs. You're seeing a lot of LPs, you know, exiting different funds at different times to get cash to fund other funds they're funding. And so that, that's just generating more trading activity. Michael Brandmeyer: So given all this illiquidity, what are you seeing with buyer and seller expectations, and does it depend on when the companies were funded? Hans Swildens: It's really interesting. I mean, there's a cohort of older companies that haven't seen acceleration. They've seen deacceleration with the AI technologies being adopted because budget's shifting away from what they were doing or maybe a lot of the AI coding technologies can kind of replace what they built. And then you're seeing the exact opposite in some older companies where they've rebuilt their tech stack to be AI first and resold that into their current customer base and seeing dramatic acceleration and adoption of their new AI technologies within their customer base, and so you're seeing hypergrowth. So, it's I'd say it's very interesting from an investment perspective because some older businesses that haven't been able to energize themselves and rearchitect their tech systems are falling behind when others are actually taking advantage of this new wave and cross-selling and upselling all the new AI that technologies have been developing to their customer base. And so that's happening. It's hard for investors to see that. And then in terms of the bar, just taking a company public today, you have to be so large. So growth has to be a certain rate. A lot of the people participating in the IPO market want to see profitability and growth metrics combined. That's just caused more pressure in terms of the companies to stay private longer. You've also had the businesses themselves and the founders decide to stay private longer in the secondary market, and the way that liquidity can be had now is enabling them to do so. And so in a weird way, our secondary market has enabled some of these companies to stay private longer because if they want to get liquidity to their employees or to their shareholders, they can do through the secondary market. And therefore, there's not a need to go to the public markets. Michael Brandmeyer: So let's orient our listeners to what is a venture secondary really mean? People talk about directs, people talk about buying portfolios, but orient us to the types of opportunities that you see in the secondary market today. Hans Swildens: Yeah, I think that's a great question. There are so many different secondary transaction types today that you can kind of bucket them into three buckets. The first bucket are direct secondary transactions, so these are single stock positions in companies or multiple stock positions in multiple companies, but they're the actual stock certificates and ownership interests in the companies that are being traded, so that's the direct secondary market, much like the Nasdaq, right? You can buy a single stock, or you can buy multiple stocks at once. And then there's the LP part of the market, which is buying limited partnership interests in the venture funds. And so the venture funds hold the same stocks that are being sold on the direct secondary market, but they're held in a fund in a commingled structure. Sometimes there's one company left, sometimes there's 50 companies left in the fund interest. But the fund interest is basically you're transacting with a limited partner that's in a fund, and then you're buying that, their ownership interest in the fund that in turn owns the company. And then the third part of the market is what I like to call special situations, which are things like continuation funds. That's a fund at the end of its life or midlife that is doing a continuation vehicle or a portfolio continuation from the vehicle itself. And basically resetting the time period. You can even reset the portfolio construction of what's being purchased in a CV or a continuation fund. Michael Brandmeyer: One of the things I find remarkable about the venture industry today is as it becomes more successful, in an interesting way, it actually becomes less liquid. I mean, today, the average company that's venture-backed that goes public takes 14 years. I mean, that's an eternity. And so you think about the venture market without the secondary market, it's almost hard to imagine right now. Hans Swildens: Yeah, I think that this has become very structural where if a limited partner or a direct shareholder or a fund manager wants to get some sort of liquidity before a normal exit of an IPO or M&A event they're looking for liquidity on the secondary market. The adoption of this from not only the smaller funds that are holding these securities at large gains, but also from the larger funds that have been in them for a long time and deployed lots of capital into them is we think is going to continue in different formats and what's largely being driven by the hold period being 14 years long. I think there's also an issue with the last five years, we've seen the amount of distributions coming out of the venture funds get over halved. So traditionally we have 20% or so per year of distributions, and we've gotten down to 5% to 10% a year on average over the last five years. So you have even more of a constraint in terms of the capital just compounding on itself and being illiquid. Michael Brandmeyer: Let's talk about your approach to pricing risk within the secondary market. I mean, this is one of the things I find really fascinating because I'm a lifelong investor and secondary investor, but I'm typically pricing cash flows. Let's start with the AI part of venture portfolios, which is growing very, very quickly right now. There's a lot of businesses that are getting funded. There is a lot of fundamental growth. There's also a lot of growth that feels like it might be a little bit secular. So, talk a little bit about how you go about pricing some of these very exciting companies which have gotten very big very quickly. How are you going about pricing these assets? Hans Swildens: I'd say the pricing exercise has been very similar to what we've been doing for two decades. In terms of venture itself compared to other asset classes has a higher component of underwriting in qualitative assessment. And so you're dealing with how large you think a market's going to be, how durable you think the product is going to be, what their competitive moat is, and how can that be extended or defended over time. It's something that has existed in technology since it started, so that's not new. I would say the thing that might be new in this phase is that we haven't seen the rapid adoption, the rapid growth, and the rapid cash flow generation and then while they're in the private market, they get disrupted. The technology shifts and changes or if something else is invented by a competitor that they might stall out and then start going negative growth while they're still private. And so it happened episodically before it wasn’t something that would happen to the whole market. You’re buying private securities, they're growing, you're seeing multiple expansion, you're seeing you know extreme valuation expansion. But then, while they're still private, you're seeing potentially contraction due to competitive threats and things. That’s new because the pace of all these new technologies has compressed the time period of success. And so it'll be interesting to see if a lot of these businesses don't go public if they're going to have really durable growth and moats over time or if they’re going to get disrupted. Michael Brandmeyer: So is that related to the analysis we talked about 30,000 companies being funded over the last maybe decade, decade and a half. Well, maybe 1000 or 2000 of them are AI funded in the last few years. That still leaves 25,000 plus that were funded effectively pre-AI. So, I guess extend that thinking into how you're analyzing the companies that were founded before AI was front of mind for everybody, including venture investors. Hans Swildens: I think there's a great investment opportunity in a small cohort of those companies where they still have amazing founders, great management teams, good technical talent, where they've been able to pivot if they're in a vertical if it's a vertically oriented SaaS business or if it's a vertically oriented services technology company. And then incorporating and building out all the new AI technologies in that vertical. They have a chance of becoming extremely fast-growing and extremely profitable, more efficient with their people in terms of just their cost structure can be less. And so I think that there's a great investment opportunity there. I think it's difficult for someone who's not in the market to assess because it's hard to see and it's hard to believe that maybe a name that people might say negative things about because they're an old business could reinvent themselves and become a great kind of hot new business, but with an old brand. But that is happening in our market, and we're starting to see some acquisitions over the last quarter. I think we saw three of that type of business for very high exit multiples because they generated new technologies and were able to, with their expertise and their knowledge of that sector and the workflows and everything, to create an application that would automate a lot of that with AI. But I would say a majority of the businesses are going to be more buyout exits, where you'll see lower growth, but higher profitability over time. And I think the tech buyout funds if they execute well, will be able to go into sectors and kind of aggregate up multiple companies in a sector and then operate them for cash flow rather than revenue growth. Michael Brandmeyer: And it's really interesting. Things are moving really quickly. Innovation is happening at a breakneck speed right now. And it also strikes me that being a risk allocator in this environment has a lot of opportunities, but also strikes me as something that's really hard. Hans Swildens: That's right. And so I think one of the things that I've appreciated over time is just portfolio construction matters and looking at your positions and risk levels in the positions, and then sizing them correctly to build like a real institutional portfolio model around risk-return, also exit timing and then your multiple by investment as well as an aggregated portfolio matters in this environment, we think more than it did before because of all the different crosscurrents and innovation going on in our market. If you can size things correctly with the risk, return hold period multiple, and an IRR assumptions, and you can get those somewhat right, then on an aggregated basis, you diversify a lot of the loss rates. Because this market has more loss rates than almost any other equity market in terms of just losing capital and transactions. Michael Brandmeyer: Let's go back to the origin story. It's in the late 1990s. This is even before you've helped create the market for venture secondaries. You're an entrepreneur. Tell us about what you were doing, what you were creating. Hans Swildens: I moved to Silicon Valley end of 1995. I started my career in the Valley sleeping on the floor of the office, doing a startup software company with my brother. I didn't have much technical experience. And so I had to learn on the job with my brother sitting next to me selling software to engineers, which was a great experience because it taught me so many different things about software development, and about engineering, and about technology. Michael Brandmeyer: And so you didn't end up being a software engineer. You ended up being effectively an asset management entrepreneur, but I'm sure those experiences were really helpful for you as you founded an investing business and started backing the types of entrepreneurs like you and your brother were before that. Hans Swildens: Yeah, I was fortunate that I had two different startups with my brother, so I was able to learn all the things we did wrong first and try to fix them in the second one, but those experiences translated really well into technology investing, understanding companies at the company level, and connecting with the entrepreneurs and the management teams at their level because that's where I came from. And that's helped me because because I could understand the risks and understand the people side of the business a little bit better than most. Michael Brandmeyer: Yeah. So after your second exit you decided to take a different path. You embarked on what became venture secondaries. As an investment strategy, talk to us about how that came about. I mean, the market didn't really exist at that moment in time. Hans Swildens: Yeah. I think the first two companies I had with my brother, too, it was very similar where we started the companies before there was a real market. That is a blessing and a curse, and so when we started investing, originally I was doing angel investing, and when the NASDAQ collapsed and the whole dot com bubble blew up, that whole capital market event caused us to relook at the venture business and see how we could make money in a very dislocated, distressed environment, and that's when we started calling and talking to other investors in the asset class and seeing if we could provide liquidity and buy them out of their positions. Michael Brandmeyer: So, Hans, this is back in the time when we got to know each other, when I was looking after our secondaries platform and you were focused on venture, and I was really intrigued by this idea. But at the time, we really didn't have the expertise or the network that you had, and it was very clear to me right away that you had a different approach to this market. Hans Swildens: I think we all had doubts of whether it was going to be, like, an episodic opportunity to create liquidity for kind of the dot-com collapse, or it would be a structural feature of the market that over time would grow. I personally thought that it was going to become something more structural over time just because the secondary market and every other market is sometimes bigger than the primary market. Most of the time it is. And so, I always had a kind of inner feeling that this market could be a lot bigger than people thought. But I'd say the first kind of five to ten years between 2000 and 2009 there were a lot of doubts in the venture business about a ten-year period of people saying, "Hey, is that just a small market opportunity that's going to go away, or is this something that structurally might develop over time into a big part of the market?" So luckily, I stuck it out and saw the market grow and compound over a long period of time and become a really massive market. Michael Brandmeyer: Yeah, I'd say it worked out just fine.  How big do you think the venture secondary market could become over time? Hans Swildens: Yeah, that's one of the things that's been really interesting being part of XIG, is this looking at the buyout market and looking at the venture growth market. I think that our division has a different kind of more on the ground perspective here. The venture and growth part of the market is becoming large. It's becoming almost the same size as the buyout market. It's getting to the point where our NAV in our market is similar. And so, we think that the venture growth market on the secondary side of the market can be larger than the primary side of the market, and we're still at a place in time today where our estimates of the venture secondary market are around a $170 billion so this year when the primary market might be, this year might even do a trillion of invested capital. And so if you look at that historically, if you average things out, the primary market's somewhere between $300 billion and $500 billion over the last five to 10 years. And so we still have a nice kind of multiple in our market to grow. In all the other asset classes, the secondary market is larger than the primary market. And so it's exciting. One thing that's interesting in our market that's starting to happen is that even participants in the secondary market are starting to get liquidity through secondaries, which historically had never happened, right? Because the secondary market didn't really exist as an option, and then it became an option, you had a situation where there was the primary market transaction and then a secondary market transaction, but you didn't have a secondary market transaction that in turn also did a secondary market transaction, and we're starting to see that happening too. So, that's the multiplier effect of why the market can be bigger than the primary market. And we're seeing that now all over the market. Michael Brandmeyer: Hans, one of the things we're seeing right now is a lot more transparency in the private markets, and so in some of these secondaries where there are employee tenders or in primary rounds, people understand the valuations, and you see more and more trades happening in the secondary market at some of these valuations. Is that leading to more volume? What is the impact on the private markets? Hans Swildens: Yeah. Historically there weren't that many transactions, right? So, it was hard to determine what the right price would be if you were a seller or if you were a buyer. And I think today with more volume and more transparency, that's just making both buyers and sellers more comfortable to transact. And so I do think that is driving more volume in the market. Michael Brandmeyer: So, I want to pivot and talk about a personal decision you made in the last year. Obviously, things have changed from the days when you had a sleeping bag under your desk and you were building companies, maybe thinking a little bit more about your rent payment and how you're going to take your girlfriend out to a nice dinner. You decided to sell Industry Ventures to Goldman Sachs a year ago. What changed over that period of time? Hans Swildens: Well, I think success changed. You know, the definition of success changes through your life. The first phase of this business, like the others, were just get it successful, right? I've always looked at businesses as like their own kind of being and their own person. So, you know, it's out of the gate, you've got to get it self-sustaining, right? It's like having your kids go off and graduate from college and get their own job and stop paying their allowance. So that was our first phase. And then I think the second phase was go execute and build out the business really well, and get it to have a nice growth rate, nice profitability, nice returns to all the LPs, nice repeatability with the investors re-upping, nice repeatability with different counterparties, with GPs, entrepreneurs, and what not, and then grow and scale it in a repeatable way, which is what we did. And then it got to a point where we had the third phase of success, which is, our market's growing, our market's institutionalizing. Should we be more institutional? Should we scale this more? If we're going to scale this more, is there a one plus one is three out there in terms of another firm like ours that's bigger, that's already built everything that we've wanted to go build in our plans? And I think luckily we found this working relationship with Goldman to be so great that over time we just sort of folded in our division. I mean, we've been working together for 20 years. You built a large part of this division from scratch and a secondary fund as well, and so there's a lot of history here. I think that that mattered. And then Goldman itself had owned part of our management company, and you saw us operate and hit our plans over a period of seven years and because we had quarterly meetings over that period, and so there just became trust during that period as well. And so, we saw this as, as a third phase of making sure that we're successful for our investors, we're successful for our team members. The business itself can be continuing to compete at an extremely high, high rate in terms of its competitiveness and kind of take this business to a next level, which I think we're doing now internally here as part of Goldman. Michael Brandmeyer: Yeah, I totally agree. And for me, it's been so much fun to bring this together. First of all, getting to know what is an absolutely terrific team of people at Industry Ventures. We've just been so impressed. Obviously, you and I have known each other for 25 years, but it's great to get to know the broader cross-section of people at Industry Ventures. And if you look at the venture secondary market, as you're saying, there's a lot more opportunity than there is capital right now. And I think that's a good backdrop for something where we can take the Goldman sourcing engine and add it to yours, which is hard to replicate with all the people that you have inside Silicon Valley with the network that you have. And so I think it's really exciting what can happen here. Let's just roll into the future here. It's 2030. What do you think this all looks like? Hans Swildens: I think it's going to look different every five years. Our market's evolved and changed, and so has all the other capital markets. Our market is kind of the driving force of AI in the world today. There are so many different opportunities, but the one area that's kind of really fascinating that's going to, we think, create a lot of opportunity is, the digital AI market and the physical AI market is going to collide. And so we're going to see a lot of things in our real life, right, be AI-enabled and live and work together with artificial intelligence in hardware formats in our daily lives. And so, there's a huge opportunity there for entrepreneurs and we're seeing a lot of innovation at the early stages there. I think you've also got healthcare is going to get transformed. It already is starting to be transformed. And then financial services and the whole re-industrialization of the United States. You're seeing the military complex being transformed right now in terms of what is being used in the battlefield. Ans then you've got space, right? So there's a bunch of opportunities now with going to the moon or interplanetary travel or everything from mining to moon base. And so, the satellite systems around the planet are obviously going to change in the next five years in a dramatic way. Michael Brandmeyer: Yeah. No shortage of excitement and change and innovation, and I can tell you I'm just so excited about working on this opportunity together in the next 5, 10, 15 years because one of the things we know for sure is there's going to be a lot of change, there's going to be a lot of innovation. And so therefore, there's going to be a lot to do. Now, Hans, we like to finish these sessions with a lightning round. So I'm going to jump into that now. What is your greatest strength as an investor? Hans Swildens: I think it's just the fact that I've worked in all different parts of our market, and I've been a player coach, and I've played every position on the field of being a founder, being an operator, being a LP, being a direct investor, being a secondary investor, being a buyout co-investor, being able to see all different sides of the coin, understanding through a life cycle of a company and a fund how liquidity works and where it might come from. And then looking at the company from a company perspective understanding how it's being operated. There's not many people I've met that have all those sets of experiences combined into one person, and so I think that's been my superpower. Michael Brandmeyer: I can remember even 15 or 20 years ago talking about your reputation here within Goldman as one of the most sober and realistic pricers of risk in the venture market. So, I would definitely agree with that. Was it easier to build software companies or a fund management business? Hans Swildens: Definitely software companies. Software companies had really quick product market fit feedback, real quick customer feedback, and then if customers liked it, and they could deploy it through their business or use it personally. You just had kind of rapid success or failure, and you could work with that easier. I think in the investment business as you know, especially with the time period to exit in our market proving out your track record, proving out you can make money, proving out you can make money at a certain IRR rate which is more important now than ever compared to other asset classes, and just proving you can invest correctly for the right risk-return for the investor base I think is really hard. It's just the duration on it's difficult. And then in terms of doing that repeatedly over cycles is very difficult cause you have drawdowns. We've had multiple drawdowns over the last 20 years and compounding capital through drawdowns is difficult. Michael Brandmeyer: What's the best piece of advice you've ever gotten? Hans Swildens: I had a good piece of advice a long time ago from a friend. He said, 'cause I asked him, "In your career, what was one of the most important things that you learned?" And he said, "Just keep doing... If you're really good at something, keep doing it for extremely long period of time. You want to be working on the same, in the same sector, on the same set of problems over a long, long period of time. And if you're really good at it and you have a talent for it, what you'll find 20, 30 years later is that you'll become an expert in that area, and everyone you've worked with during that period of time, plus the people they know, will come to you for a solution or advice or in our case, investing opportunities.” Michael Brandmeyer: And finally, what are you excited about in the world right now? Hans Swildens: I think this is one of the most exciting times I've ever seen for investing. It's like all the innovation across every category in the world. It's a worldwide innovation event. It's a platform shift and I think we're just beginning in it across all sectors. And so, I couldn't think of a more exciting time that I've ever seen in the technology markets in my life. Michael Brandmeyer: I agree. Hans, thanks for being with us today. Michael Brandmeyer: Thank you for listening to this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors, which was recorded on Tuesday, September 8th, 2026. I'm Michael Brandmeyer.  shares have slipped more than a fifth below the record peak reached in July, pulling the Wall Street powerhouse into bear-market territory just days before it is due to report quarterly results. The slide has been driven by cautious expectations for bond trading revenue and by the Federal Reserve finalizing updated stress-testing rules for large banks. The pullback is notable because the stock had been one of the standout performers among large financial names for much of the year, powered by a revival in advisory work and strong equity trading. A decline of this size over a few months has shifted the conversation from momentum to resilience, with market participants asking how much of the recent weakness is already reflected in the share price. Goldman Sachs is a global financial institution best known for advising corporations and governments, underwriting securities and making markets. Its global banking and markets division houses the advisory, underwriting and trading businesses that have historically defined the firm and driven much of its revenue. A second major segment, asset and wealth management, manages money for institutions, sovereign clients and wealthy families. In recent years management has worked to make this arm a larger and steadier contributor, aiming to complement the more cyclical earnings of the trading and advisory units. Bond, currency and commodity trading is a major source of revenue at Goldman Sachs, and expectations for the latest quarter have turned more guarded. Bond markets have been unsettled by the climb in Treasury yields, and some clients have stepped back from large positioning, leaving volumes less certain than the strong tape of recent periods. Trading desks typically thrive on volatility that is orderly, meaning enough movement to generate client flow without the disorder that discourages activity. The recent rise in yields has produced movement, yet the speed of the shift has left some desks cautious about how much client activity translated into revenue. The Federal Reserve finalizing updated stress-testing rules has added a layer of regulatory attention to the group. These annual exercises determine how much capital each large bank must maintain, and in turn influence how much it can distribute to stockholders through dividends and buybacks. For Goldman Sachs, the details matter because its capital requirements are sensitive to the size of its trading and underwriting exposures. Changes to the way those exposures are measured can shift the buffer the firm must keep, affecting both its flexibility and the pace of capital distributions. On the brighter side, the advisory and underwriting pipelines have been described by bankers as healthy. Corporate boards have shown a renewed willingness to pursue mergers and acquisitions, and companies have returned to the equity and debt markets after a period of hesitation. Goldman Sachs ranks among the leading advisers on large global transactions, which tends to put it at the front of the line when deal activity improves. Fee revenue from these mandates is recognized when deals close, so the timing of completions can influence results from one quarter to the next. The equities franchise has been a pillar of recent strength. Client demand for financing, derivatives and prime brokerage services has stayed strong, reflecting active hedge fund and institutional participation in global stock markets. Prime services in particular generate steadier revenue because they earn fees and financing spreads on client balances. As client balances have grown alongside rising asset prices, the business has become a larger part of the firm's overall earnings. Financial Stocks have attracted fresh attention this week as the large banks prepare to report, with interest focused on how different business models are faring. Deposit-rich lenders have benefited from stable funding, while capital-markets-oriented firms have been more exposed to the swings of trading and deal flow. Competition among Wall Street firms is fierce. JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley contest many of the same advisory and trading mandates, and Bank of America and Citigroup compete in underwriting and global markets. Boutique advisory shops have also gained share in some deal categories. Technology plays a growing role in the business. The firm has been rolling out generative artificial intelligence tools to its workforce, aiming to speed up tasks such as drafting documents, summarizing research and writing code. The broader market backdrop has been mixed. Equity benchmarks including the S&P 500 have remained near elevated levels, supporting asset values and wealth-management fees, while higher Treasury yields have weighed on bond prices and added caution to some corners of the market. Goldman Sachs is scheduled to release results next week alongside the other large banks. Market participants will watch advisory and underwriting fees, equities and bond trading revenue, asset and wealth management results and the trend in expenses. With the stock well below its July peak, expectations have shifted, and the report is likely to be treated as a test of how much of the recent caution was warranted. title: Mikaela Shiffrin Plans Fewer Slaloms to Chase GS and Super-G - Ski Racing Media
content: Image Credit: “What’s the Point, Presented by Stifel” Mikaela Shiffrin plans to race fewer slaloms in 2026-27 and devote more training time to giant slalom and super-G. Her current plan calls for her first slalom start at Killington, followed by selected races through the winter. For the Stifel U.S. Ski Team athlete, the change begins with a question: Where does she most want to improve? In the video below, Shiffrin calls the coming winter an “exploration season.” After 16 years, she wants to give the disciplines that now spark her curiosity more room in her program. The decision follows a season in which she earned her ninth World Cup slalom title and reached 110 career World Cup victories. It changes how she will divide her training and racing time while she remains at the top of slalom. Shiffrin describes the moments that keep drawing her back to skiing: a turn that does not work, a conversation about why and the breakthrough that follows. Right now, GS and super-G offer the questions she most wants to answer. Last season, she says, she initially worried about losing her place among the top 30 in GS. Working back into the top seven showed her that she could find speed while still confronting fear. That experience helped renew her interest in what comes next. She wants dedicated training blocks to explore those possibilities, with fewer switches between disciplines. Slalom demands its own sustained preparation. Shiffrin says the coordination, reaction speed, physical effort and repetition require maximum attention. Reducing that training carries consequences, even for her. “One does not simply show up to any World Cup race and win,” she says. Under her current plan, Shiffrin would skip the early slaloms in Levi and Gurgl before returning to the discipline at Killington, Vermont, an Ikon Pass destination. She then intends to select additional slaloms. Maintaining her ranking matters because she wants the option to shift her focus again if she misses the discipline. The schedule also creates short windows for recovery and body maintenance. An early-season visit home could give her time with family and her new niece — an opportunity she rarely gets during the racing winter. Shiffrin cautions that her overall race load may look much the same once the season gets underway. The biggest difference could come in the first third of the winter, along with how she uses the time between races. Longevity runs through her explanation. Shiffrin says conversations after her Cortina injury helped her recognize that trying to do everything throughout an entire career might be unsustainable. Now she wants to see whether a different balance can help her continue doing the work she loves. “I’m not trying to do less because I care less,” she says. “I’m trying to do something different because I still care so much.” She acknowledges concern about disappointing fans and supporters. But she also says the people closest to her have encouraged her to choose what is best for her. Her plan leaves the outcome open. More focused training could reveal new possibilities in GS and super-G. Selected slalom starts could pull her back toward that discipline. title: ZXMoto is working BMW R1300 GS rivaling big-bore boxer twin - Visordown
content: ZXMoto has unveiled a working shaft drive boxer twin of around 1,000cc, with 100bhp. Two years after its founding, the Chinese brand is eyeing BMW's best-selling adventure bike. The burgeoning Chinese brand, ZXMoto, seems to be pushing in every available direction, with sports bikes, nakeds, lightweight off-roaders, rally bikes and more. If it’s got two wheels and an engine, ZXMoto wants to have a crack at building it. Its latest revelation, though, might see the brand going toe-to-toe with the biggest and best-selling adventure bike of the last twenty years. The company’s founder, Zhang Xue (hence the ‘ZX’ in the brand’s name), has revealed a new engine unlike anything in the existing range. Clearly a boxer twin, the company first teased the new engine at EICMA in 2025. Back then, it was nothing more than a rendering and a dream. Fast forward to today, and it’s fully designed and built, and seemingly ready to slot into a new bike. Presenting the engine at CIMA 2026, Zhang Xue showed off an apparently fully working and developed engine with a capacity of around 1,000cc. While the official specification of the engine remains unknown at the time of writing, reports from China suggest it has an output north of 100bhp, liquid cooling, and chain-driven cams, as per the latest generation of boxer twins from BMW. Like the BMW engine, the ZXMoto powerplant features a longitudinal layout, with an output shaft at the rear of the engine. That is obviously priming it for a shaft drive to the rear wheel, a feature that has become a mainstay of BMW’s sports touring and adventure bikes. And while a boxer twin of around 1,000cc and more than 100bhp isn’t groundbreaking in itself, it’s the speed of development that is the more interesting part of this story. ZXMoto was only officially founded in 2024. By 2025, it was presenting new bikes at EICMA, racing, and winning in the WorldSSP championship, while also showing off new engines and technologies. Now, just two years after the company was formed, it has a working large-capacity boxer twin that appears to be designed with a shaft-driven motorcycle in mind. That is a fairly clear statement of intent. There is also the question of what happens next. ZXMoto has shown that it can move from an idea to a production-ready engine remarkably quickly, and a boxer twin opens up more possibilities than just one adventure bike. A shaft-driven sport tourer, road bike or even a large-capacity naked could all make use of the same basic powerplant. What we do know is that the company has gone from showing a computer-generated boxer twin at EICMA 2025 to displaying a working engine at CIMA 2026. TOKYO, October 5, 2026 – Goldman Sachs Japan Co., Ltd. announced today that Shigeru Ariizumi has joined Goldman Sachs as an International Advisor, effective October 1, 2026. Mr. Ariizumi began his career at Japan’s Ministry of Finance in 1988 and subsequently served in senior positions at the Ministry of Finance, the Financial Services Agency (FSA), the Japan Fair Trade Commission, and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). He held a number of key leadership roles, primarily within the Ministry of Finance’s Budget Bureau and International Bureau and at the FSA, before retiring from public service in July 2025 as Vice Minister for International Affairs at the Financial Services Agency. During this distinguished career, he represented Japan at the deputy vice finance minister level at the G7 and G20, and was responsible for foreign exchange markets and the management of Japan’s foreign exchange reserves. He also served as Chair of the Executive Committee of the International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS) and Vice Chairman of the Board of the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO). Since February 2026, he has served as Special Counsel at Mori Hamada, and is admitted to practice law in both Japan and New York. International Advisors are external experts appointed by Goldman Sachs globally to provide strategic insights and advice to the firm's leadership and clients on political, economic, regulatory, and industry developments. Mr. Ariizumi possesses deep knowledge of the global macroeconomic landscape and the implications of economic and policy developments for financial markets and the Japanese economy. He also has broad experience and insight into the evolution of international financial regulatory frameworks and the practical implementation of financial supervision and regulation in Japan. Goldman Sachs has appointed Mr. Ariizumi as its first International Advisor in Japan, recognizing the depth of expertise and breadth of perspective he brings to the role. Going forward, he will provide strategic counsel on the firm's business priorities and its response to evolving market and regulatory developments. Hidehiro Imatsu, President and Representative Director of Goldman Sachs Japan Co., Ltd., said, "We are honored to welcome Shigeru Ariizumi as an International Advisor to Goldman Sachs. Throughout his career, he has made significant contributions to the development of financial and capital market frameworks and to international regulatory cooperation, both in Japan and globally. At a time of heightened geopolitical uncertainty, evolving regulatory expectations, and ongoing transformation of Japan's corporate governance and capital markets, his unparalleled expertise in financial policy, regulation, and international affairs will be an invaluable asset as we continue to deliver the highest level of service to our clients." Mr. Ariizumi said, “I am delighted to have been appointed as an International Advisor at Goldman Sachs. At a time when the global economy and international financial markets continue to undergo significant change, I look forward to drawing on my experience to provide value-added advice to the firm, a leader in global finance. Through these efforts, I hope to contribute to raising the global profile of Japan’s financial sector and further strengthening its ties with the international financial community.” The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. is a leading global financial institution that delivers a broad range of financial services to a large and diversified client base that includes corporations, financial institutions, governments and individuals. title: 10 Motorcycles That Make More Sense Used Than New - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update A new motorcycle offers fresh parts, full break-in control, and zero worry about past abuse. Still, buying brand-new often makes little financial sense once you factor in dealer fees, destination charges, and immediate showroom-floor depreciation. Conversely, the used market offers incredible value if you take the time to hunt. Great bargains span every category, from commuters and cruisers to adventure tourers and exotics. Going pre-owned is also the only way to own celebrated models that manufacturers have discontinued. Here are 10 standout motorcycles that offer exceptional value and make far more sense bought used rather than new. The DR650S is the kind of motorcycle you would want with you once a world war breaks out, because it is simple and makes reliability feel effortless. The only electronic item on it is the digital ignition; other than that, everything is analog and can be worked on with a basic toolbox. It runs a simple air-cooled, SOHC, four-valve, single-cylinder, carbureted engine with a displacement of 644 cc. It makes 43.5 horsepower and 39.8 pound-feet of torque. It puts this down through a five-speed gearbox and drive chain to the wheel. It does not have tubeless tires, ABS, or LED lighting. All it has is long-travel suspension with adjustable preload and compression damping for the rear shock. You can also have it fitted with a lowering kit at the dealer level. It has not changed for decades, which, along with its reliability, means you can have a used one with all the benefits of a new one. The VFR1200F is a model coming up on 20 years of age, but if you pick one near the end of its run, you can have one that is around 13 years old for less than the price of most middleweight naked bikes. To remind you, this is a full-size sport-tourer that balances touring comfort with everyday practicality. It also lays claim to having the world's first dual-clutch automatic transmission for a motorcycle. The first generation had slightly clunky gear shifts, but with revisions, the gearbox became a lot smoother. That is not the only interesting thing about the VFR1200F. The engine is a V4, but it has a unique layout in that the inner cylinders make up the rear-facing bank so that the motorcycle is narrow at the rider’s seat. It generated 170 horsepower and 95.1 pound-feet of torque from its 1,237 cc engine. You could have either the automatic or a six-speed manual, and a driveshaft means that you do not have to worry about chain maintenance or the condition of the sprockets. Harley-Davidson took a big risk when it chose to convert its Sportster series to modern cruisers that had more in common with street bikes than traditional Milwaukee cruisers. They are lighter, quicker, and have a more reliable liquid-cooled engine, but Harley traditionalists do not like them very much. The Sportster Iron 883 was the last of the air-cooled Sportsters, and it walked a fine line between the heritage of the brand and attracting new customers with its performance. The Evolution series engine displaced 883 cc like the name suggests, and it generated 54 horsepower and 53.8 pound-feet of torque. These numbers might look modest, especially when you consider it had a five-speed gearbox, but the Iron 883 offered all the right sensations, not to mention the fact that it was extremely customizable. Its popularity has led The Motor Co. to confirm that the Sportster 883 will return in 2027. Meanwhile, you can have one of the older ones for an extremely reasonable price. The SV650 has led a charmed life. It started out as a more reasonably priced version of a very popular Italian naked motorcycle, and it has somehow outlasted that motorcycle by an incredible number of years. It sells so well even now that Suzuki recently updated it with ABS, and the engine has received a massive update in another model to keep up with tightening emissions regulations globally. This speaks volumes for the popularity of this 90-degree V-twin. It has liquid cooling and four valves per cylinder and generates 73 horsepower and 47.2 pound-feet from 645 cc in its current form in the SV. It does not run a by-wire throttle, and neither does this motorcycle have a six-axis IMU. All you have is good looks, affordable maintenance, and the ability to upgrade it any which way you desire with the help of a very strong community of owners. This is the kind of motorcycle that quietly builds lifelong owners, so it is rare to find one used. The FJR is one of the old-school sport-touring motorcycles with an inline-four engine with large displacement tuned for torque coupled with shaft drive. Here, the engine displaces 1,298 cc and makes 146 horsepower and a massive 101.8 pound-feet of torque, which means gear shifts are almost optional and adding a pillion and luggage has no effect on the pulling power of the FJR. It has been the same for over a decade, and it has been sold in the US market as the FJR1300ES, with the ES designating the electronic suspension. It is not short on safety either, since it offers ride modes, linked brakes with ABS, traction control, cruise control, and cornering LED lamps. The conveniences include luggage that does not need a different key to operate and adjustable heating for the heated grips. A new one costs nearly $20,000, and given its reliability, bargain hunters are snatching it up. The Boulevard M109R, like the Suzuki SV650, has been the same for an incredibly long time, and it is still available as a new motorcycle today. In fact, at its new price, you get the most powerful cruiser available for under $20,000, which makes it incredible value for money. There have been zero updates during its run, so while the case for buying it new exists, the case for buying it used is much stronger. That is because of its massive 54-degree V-twin that displaces 1,783 cc and generates 123 horsepower and a monstrous 118 pound-feet of torque. It sends this through a wide-ratio five-speed gearbox and a driveshaft to the wheel. Its brooding styling has aged quite well, and it has the basics down with inverted front forks, sportbike-spec front brakes, and a tachometer mounted on the handlebar right in the rider's line of sight. We do not deny that ABS and traction control would be wonderful additions despite one of the widest rear tires on a production motorcycle, but it is also extremely reliable, giving you a 20-year-old metric cruiser that makes new Harley-Davidsons sweat for even less. The Low Rider S is a relatively young motorcycle in its current version, since it was launched in 2022 with the Milwaukee-Eight 117 High Output engine. This engine displaces 1,923 cc and generates 114 horsepower and 128 pound-feet of torque, and puts it down through a six-speed transmission. You could also shave off some of the acquisition price by going for the 2020 or 2021 model year Low Rider S, but you would also have to give up some power and torque because it was powered by the older Milwaukee-Eight 114 engine. You would not miss out on anything else, though, because even the older model had inverted front forks and dual front disc brakes that genuinely helped it achieve much better pace. However, this is the cruiser that quietly gets better every year, which means that it can be quite confusing choosing the right model. In 2025, it got a six-axis IMU, but it had optional and later standard traction control for 2023 and 2024, and the model powered by the Milwaukee-Eight 114 had only dual-channel ABS. Still, this is an extremely reliable sport cruiser, and it has a premium badge on the tank, which means premium levels of depreciation. Yamaha was making muscle cruisers way before they were a thing in the eyes of Harley-Davidson or Ducati, and the V-Max is what every fan of the power cruiser will gravitate toward. The first-generation model had an awesome run, but the second-generation model has unbeatable performance, so that is the preference of everyone who wants one. That shows up in its extremely high residual values as well, and it deserves a second life. However, it would never pass today's emissions tests in the state of tune it was in. The second-generation V-Max's V4 displaced 1,679 cc and made an incredible 197 horsepower and 123 pound-feet of torque. The first- and second-generation V-Max models put together were on sale for three and a half decades, and it has built up a loyal following thanks to reliability that matches its performance. That performance was backed by electronics: the second gen had a by-wire throttle, variable-length intake funnels, an aluminum chassis that used the engine as a stressed member, fully adjustable front forks, a link-type monoshock rear suspension, and dual 320 mm front brake discs with massive six-piston calipers each. The V-Max was born for the drag strip and can still do wonders on it today. The Pan America is probably the most un-Harley-like Harley-Davidson in history, with its high-revving, liquid-cooled engine with variable valve timing on all its valves, the chassis that uses the engine as a stressed member, its long-travel suspension, and its final chain drive. What aligns with the brand is that this is a premium product with all the technology that you would expect from something with the Bar and Shield on the fuel tank. You can have it in different flavors, but the Pan America 1250 Special is a good intersection of value and ability. Because it has cross-spoke tubeless rims, it has the ability to go further off-road, and it is also equipped with electronic suspension that lowers it at walking pace, which makes it a lot easier to ride in the city. Out on the highway is where it is in its element, of course, with its 1,252 cc Revolution Max V-twin engine making good use of its 150 horsepower and 95 pound-feet of torque. This is also the only Harley-Davidson with a two-way quickshifter, but the assist-and-slipper clutch will prove its worth in traffic as well. It depreciates quite heavily, so it makes a lot more sense used than new, getting you a modern, well-equipped adventure tourer for a lot less than its new price. Of the full-size premium adventure touring motorcycles, BMW's flagship GS has always been the one to beat, despite having almost nothing in common with others in its segment. It uses the Telelever and Paralever suspension, which is unique to it. It sticks with its horizontal boxer-twin longitudinal engine with a driveshaft, and it has all the electronics you could possibly want. You do have to pay handsomely for the privilege of owning a GS, not just in terms of the upfront purchase price but also service costs, but the previous-generation R 1250 GS costs less to own than you expect. The sweet spot is the version launched in 2021, as that is when the R 1250 GS was equipped with a six-axis IMU as standard equipment; any packages added above that were software unlocks. This engine displaced 1,254 cc and generated 136 horsepower and 105.4 pound-feet of torque, which is competitive even today. It also had a 6.5-inch TFT instrument cluster and an all-LED headlamp, and there is a good chance you will get one with BMW's packages installed, which is why it holds such good residual values. title: GS Entec to supply 37 monopiles for Taean wind project - Ocean Energy Resources
content: GLOBAL NEWS SERVICE FOR THE FOSSIL AND RENEWABLE ENERGY COMMUNITIES GS Entec, based in Ulsan South Korea, will supply 37 monopiles for the 504-megawatt Taean offshore wind farm off the coast of Taean, South Chungcheong Province. Under a contract signed Wednesday at Taean Wind Power’s Seoul headquarters, GS Entec will begin production in July 2027 and complete deliveries by the end of August 2028. The Taean offshore wind project is being jointly developed by Singapore-based renewable energy developer Vena Energy, Danish infrastructure investor Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners and Korea Western Power. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028 and finish in 2030. Once completed, the farm is expected to power about 300,000 households for a year. GS Entec entered the monopile business in 2022 through a strategic technology partnership with Dutch company Sif. It supplied all 64 monopiles for the Yeonggwang Nakwol offshore wind project in 2023 and has since secured the Taean project. The company is one of the few in South Korea with experience mass-producing and delivering large monopiles from a single domestic plant. title: Unpopular Opinion: Karol G’s Karol G Tropitour Was for the Latina Who Cried Through ‘Mañana Será Bonito’ and Needed to Know She Made It Through - BELatina
content:
The Karol G Viajando por el Mundo Tropitour concert in Miami almost did not happen for me, and I say that knowing full well how different this story would feel if it had not. An opportunity came through Acoustyle and I decided to take it, bringing my Colombian friend Angélica Romero along, a paisa from Medellín and a costeña from Barranquilla navigating the aggressively humid Miami streets together on a night that turned out to be a lot more than either of us had anticipated. The heat that greeted us outside was the type that slaps you across the face and reminds you exactly where you are, and somehow it was perfect because we were already feeling tropical before we even walked through the doors, already carrying that specific electricity that comes from being two Colombian women about to watch a Colombian woman own a stage. It is worth being honest about the hesitation that many Karol G fans felt going into the Tropitour era, because I felt it too. After Mañana Sera Bonito, which functioned as collective healing for women in a way that felt less like a concert and more like therapy, some of us were still craving that specific hug from her music, the one that spoke directly to the broken parts of Latinas and made us feel seen in our pain. Tropicoqueta is a different energy, and at first that difference felt disorienting, like being handed something bright and colorful when part of you was still holding on to something tender. But standing in that crowd in Miami, sweating through a sexy outfit, holding a cold drink dripping down my arm while singing every word, I understood it completely. Latinas are multifaceted, and we are not always in our healing era. Sometimes we are in our tropical, fully alive era, and Karol G was giving us permission to inhabit that version of ourselves without guilt or apology. To understand what the Tropitour meant to me, you have to understand what Mañana Sera Bonito did to me first. That era saved me in ways I am still processing, arriving during one of the hardest periods of my life, a year where everything felt so heavy that I genuinely was not sure I was going to make it through emotionally. Karol G’s voice was on repeat constantly, and I was praying and daydreaming for a day when I would feel whole again, playing her album like a promise I was making to myself that the day would come. The fact that she is Colombian, from Medellín, the same city as me, made her feel like a sister in those moments, like someone who understood without needing to be told, and that closeness carried me through more dark nights than I want to count. Because the album meant so much to me, I made it a point to join her Mañana Sera Bonito show in Miami, putting on the sparkles, getting all cute and walking into Hard Rock Stadium with a heavy heart but ready to be there for every second of it. Music has a way of creating intimacy with people you will probably never meet, and sometimes a voice and a melody is proximity enough to make you feel less alone in what you are going through, which is exactly what that night was supposed to be for me. But when “Amargura” came on and I felt everything in my chest rise to the surface at once, I slipped out of my seat and let the moment pass without me, protecting myself from a grief I was not ready to feel in public. I carried that unfinished feeling without even knowing it was still there, tucked underneath everything else, waiting for the right moment to finally let it breathe. When Karol G came out at the Tropitour, her energy moved through the crowd before I even had time to prepare myself for it, and the next thing I knew I was fully in it, moving and singing and feeling every bit of the tropical night she had built around us, the version of myself from the Mañana Sera Bonito era feeling very far away in the best possible sense. She moved through her original songs before inviting people onto the stage to dance with her, including two Cubans she mentioned were among the first Cubans she had ever brought on stage, a Mexican and two Colombians, and there was something about watching all of us come together in that moment for a good perreo to “Bby Wow” that felt like a celebration of everything live music is supposed to be, a room full of people from different places finding the same joy at the same time. What made it even more special was that she incorporated TikTok videos of fans doing the Bby Wow trend into the show, which said everything about how she and her team operate because they are genuinely paying attention to what is happening around her influence and they are choosing to honor it rather than take it for granted, and that attentiveness is one of the things that separates Karol G from artists who simply perform for their audience rather than with them. That same spirit showed up when she brought out mariachis, then Elena Rose and Greeicy, giving the stage to artists who are still building their moment in a way that not every artist at her level chooses to do, and watching her create space for others when she has worked so hard to create space for herself felt like its own lesson. By the time she performed “Bichota” with cumbia influences, the song felt like it had grown alongside everyone in that crowd, like we were all moving closer to our folkloric roots together, because somewhere underneath all the perreo we have always been craving that sound and the Tropitour feels like Karol G’s way of telling us we are allowed to want it all. In the middle of the concert, the flames going off next to us were adding an extra layer of heat to an already sweltering night when “Amargura” came on. I heard the first few notes and my body knew before my brain did, and everything I had been carrying from the last time I heard that song live came rushing back in an instant. The last time I had heard it live I had to leave the room because I was not ready for what it was going to bring out of me, and this time I stayed, sang every word, danced to it and let myself feel joy inside a song that once felt too heavy to inhabit, and somewhere in the middle of all of that I realized that the unfinished moment I had been carrying since the Mañana Sera Bonito tour had finally been completed. It was the full circle I did not know I was walking toward when I almost skipped this concert entirely. Karol G moves through eras constantly but she is someone whose music always accounts for what is in your heart and walks alongside you whether you are broken or thriving or somewhere in the complicated space between the two, and the Tropitour is proof that she has never stopped doing that even as the sound has changed. We can be emotional bichotas with a matadora energy and still have time to sing “Pineapple” and “Mamiii” because we contain all of it, and Karol G has been telling us that unapologetically through every genre she touches. Standing in that crowd in Miami, finally singing “Amargura” without having to leave the room, I understood that the healing she started with me during Mañana Sera Bonito was never really over. title: JPM, GS, MS Stocks Edge Higher After-Hours — Banks Lift Dividends And Announce Buybacks After Fed Stress Test - Stocktwits
content: Shares of JPMorgan Chase & Co (JPM), Morgan Stanley (MS) and Goldman Sachs (GS) edged higher in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the banks announced higher dividends and buybacks following the Federal Reserve’s stress test, which showed the banking sector remains well positioned to withstand a severe economic downturn. At the time of writing, JPM stock was up 0.6% after-hours after closing the regular session down 0.21%, while MS shares gained 0.4% and GS stock was up 0.1%. JPMorgan Chase & Co announced a $50-billion share repurchase program and raised its quarterly dividend as part of updated shareholder return plans. The bank said its board also intends to increase its quarterly dividend 10% to $1.65 per share, up from $1.50 per share, for the third quarter of 2026. The new buyback program will take effect from July 1, alongside the updated shareholder return plans. Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO of JPMorgan Chase, said, “The Board’s intended dividend increase is supported by our consistent investment in our business and strong financial performance. The new share repurchase program provides us with the flexibility to deploy capital in ways that enhance shareholder value over time.” Goldman Sachs (GS) also increased its quarterly dividend by 11% to $5 per share from $4.50, pointing to strong earnings momentum and a robust capital position. The revised payout implies an annual dividend of $20 and will take effect on July 1, pending board approval. Morgan Stanley (MS) similarly announced a 15% hike in its quarterly dividend to $1.15 per share from $1. In addition, the firm said its board has reauthorized a multi-year share repurchase program of up to $20 billion, with no fixed end date, set to begin in the third quarter. The announcement by JPMorgan Chase & Co comes after the U.S. Federal Reserve released the results of its annual stress test. It showed that large banks are well positioned to withstand a severe recession and continue lending to households and businesses. The Fed said that despite more than $708 billion in total loan losses under the hypothetical scenario, aggregate capital declined only 1.6 percentage points and remained above minimum requirements. It added that all 32 banks tested stayed above their minimum common equity tier 1 capital requirements under a scenario that included a severe global recession, a 39% drop in commercial real estate prices, a 30% fall in house prices and an unemployment rate peaking at 10%.
